title: Top 5 Weirdest Ways Animals Sleep 😴
hook: You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these 5 animals do it.
script:
You think you sleep badly? Wait until you see how these five animals do it.
We're counting down to the strangest sleeper on the planet.
Number five: sea otters.
They float on their backs and often hold paws, so they don't drift apart.
Number four: sperm whales.
They nap upright, like giant floating pillars, for just ten to fifteen minutes.
Number three: the common swift.
This bird can stay airborne for about ten months straight, and scientists think it naps up there.
Number two: frigatebirds.
Researchers caught them sleeping mid-flight, in bursts of about twelve seconds.
That adds up to less than an hour a day.
Number one: wild African elephants.
A study found they sleep only about two hours a day, mostly standing up.
So the strangest sleeper of all? The giant that barely sleeps.
Which one sleeps most like you? Comment below.
And next time you think you sleep badly, wait until you see how these five animals do it.

title: 5 Funny Town Names With Wild Backstories

script:
These five real town names sound made up, but you could drive to every single one of them.
Every name has a true story.
Number five: Accident, Maryland.
Two survey teams in the seventeen-fifties measured the same land by mistake. Hence, Accident.
Number four: Hot Coffee, Mississippi.
A shop owner sold hot coffee to travelers, and the town took the name.
Number three: Why, Arizona.
It sits where two highways form a Y. But names needed at least three letters, so Y became W-H-Y.
Number two: Truth or Consequences, New Mexico.
In nineteen-fifty, a radio show offered to broadcast from any town that took its name. Hot Springs said yes.
Number one: Boring, Oregon.
It's officially partnered with Dull, Scotland, and Bland, Australia. Yes, really.
So the funniest name? Boring. Which is anything but.

title: The Great Rubber Duck Escape of 1992 🦆
hook: A storm knocked 28,800 bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
script:
A storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship, and they ended up teaching you how the ocean moves.
Here's how they became a science experiment.
It's January, nineteen ninety-two.
A cargo ship from Hong Kong hits a storm in the North Pacific.
Containers tumble into the sea, and one is full of plastic toys.
Yellow ducks, blue turtles, red beavers and green frogs.
The box breaks, and they float away.
Ten months later, the first ones wash up in Alaska.
Ocean scientist Curtis Ebbesmeyer gets curious.
He asks beachcombers to report every toy.
Each sighting shows where the currents carried them.
Some circled the North Pacific in a giant loop of current, and some may have drifted into the Arctic ice.
So a lost box of bath toys helped map how the ocean moves.
Found one on the beach? What would you name it? Tell me below.
Because a storm knocked twenty-eight thousand eight hundred bath toys off a ship…

title: 3 School Facts That Are Actually False
hook: 3 facts you probably still believe, and you have 3 seconds to guess which are false.
script:
Three facts you probably still believe, and you have three seconds to guess which are false.
Say true or false out loud before the timer runs out.
Fact one: goldfish only remember things for three seconds.
Three, two, one.
False! Scientists have trained goldfish to respond to sounds and remember them for months.
Fact two: you can see the Great Wall of China from space with your bare eyes.
Three, two, one.
False again! From orbit it's very hard to spot, because it's narrow and the same color as the land around it.
Fact three: bulls get angry when they see the color red.
Three, two, one.
Also false! Bulls can't see red the way you do. It's the cape's movement that gets their attention.
So the answer: all three are false.

title: 3 Memory Tricks to Remember Anything
hook: If you've ever forgotten someone's name 5 seconds after hearing it, you need these 3 tricks.
script:
If you've ever forgotten someone's name five seconds after hearing it, you need these three tricks.
They come from real memory research.
Trick one: test yourself instead of rereading.
In one famous study, students who quizzed themselves remembered more a week later than students who just reread.
Meet someone? Say their name back, then recall it a minute later.
Trick two: chunk it.
Your brain juggles only a handful of things at once, so phone numbers come in little groups.
Long code? Shopping list? Break it into chunks of three or four.
Trick three: build a memory palace.
Picture your home, and put each thing you want to remember in a different room.
Memory champions use it, and in one study, regular people who practiced got way better at lists.
That's the set: test yourself, chunk it, and build a memory palace.
Which trick are you trying first? Tell me in the comments.
Because if you've ever forgotten someone's name five seconds after hearing it…

title: Is That Really What I Sound Like?
hook: You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
script:
You've never actually heard your own voice. Not once. Here's why.
Not the way everyone else hears it, and it's down to your skull.
When you talk, your voice reaches your ears in two ways.
First, through the air, just like any other sound.
Second, through your own head. The vibrations travel through the bones of your skull, straight to your inner ear.
And bone is great at carrying the low, deep parts of your voice.
So to you, your voice sounds richer and a bit deeper.
A recording only catches the air part. No skull, no extra bass.
That's why it sounds higher and thinner, and kind of not like you.
So, is that really what you sound like? Yes. The recording is much closer to what your friends hear every day.
And that voice you cringe at? They already love it.
Be honest, do you skip your own voice messages? Tell me in the comments.
Because you've never actually heard your own voice…

title: 5 Peppers That Make Jalapeños Look Mild
hook: You think jalapeños are hot? The pepper at number one is hundreds of times hotter.
script:
You think jalapeños are hot? The pepper at number one is hundreds of times hotter.
Let's count down five peppers that make a jalapeño look mild.
Pepper heat is measured in Scoville units, and a jalapeño is only a few thousand.
Number five: the habanero. Up to around three hundred fifty thousand.
Already way too much for most people.
Number four: the ghost pepper. Around one million.
It was the first pepper ever measured over a million.
Number three: the Trinidad Moruga Scorpion. Around one point two million, with a little stinger-like tail.
Number two: the Carolina Reaper. About one point six million.
It held the world record for about ten years.
Number one: Pepper X. About two point seven million.
That's the hottest pepper in the world, according to Guinness.
Please, admire these with your eyes, not your mouth.
What's the hottest thing you've ever eaten? Tell me below.
And if you think jalapeños are hot…

title: 3 Tricks to Cut Onions Without Crying
hook: You're probably making the onion tears worse, and here's how to fix it with 3 tricks.
script:
You're probably making the onion tears worse, and here's how to fix it with three tricks.
First, the reason it happens.
When you cut an onion, you break open its cells.
That sets off a reaction that makes a stingy gas.
It floats up, hits your eyes, and your eyes make tears to wash it out.
Trick one: chill it first.
Pop it in the fridge before cutting. Cold slows the reaction, so less gas reaches your eyes.
Trick two: use a really sharp knife.
A dull knife crushes the onion, and crushed cells release more of the stuff. A sharp blade slices clean.
Trick three: leave the root end for last.
That part is packed with more of the tear-making compounds, so cut around it.
That's it: chill it, sharpen it, and save the root for last.
Bonus: swimming goggles. They work, and look hilarious.
Which trick are you trying next time? Tell me below.

One idea is grip.
In one experiment, wrinkly fingers moved wet marbles between boxes faster.
Kind of like tire treads on a rainy road.

title: Is a Banana a Berry? 3-Second Quiz
hook: You'll never look at a fruit bowl the same way. 3 fruits, 3 seconds each: berry or not?
script:
You'll never look at a fruit bowl the same way. Three fruits, three seconds each: berry or not?
Here's the rule botanists use, then we test it.
A true berry grows from one flower's single ovary, seeds inside the soft flesh.
Fruit one: the banana. Berry or not? Three, two, one.
Berry! One ovary, with tiny seeds right in the middle.
Fruit two: the strawberry. Three, two, one.
Not a berry! Each little dot on the outside is its own tiny fruit.
Fruit three: the avocado. Three, two, one.
Berry! Botanists call it a single-seeded berry, big seed and all.
Bonus: raspberries aren't true berries either. Each bead is like a tiny stone fruit.
And by the same rule, tomatoes and grapes count as berries too.
So the answers are berry, not a berry, and berry.
How many did you get right: zero, one, two, or three? Tell me in the comments.

title: How an 11-Year-Old Invented the Popsicle
hook: You've eaten one, but did you know an 11-year-old invented the popsicle by forgetting his drink in 1905?
script:
You've eaten one, but did you know an eleven-year-old invented the popsicle by forgetting his drink in nineteen-oh-five?
Here's how one forgotten cup became a summer favorite.
His name was Frank Epperson, from San Francisco.
One winter day, the story goes, he mixed soda powder with water.
He stirred it with a little wooden stick.
Then he left the cup on the porch, stick and all, and forgot it.
That night it got cold, and by morning the drink had frozen solid.
Frank ran the cup under warm water, pulled the stick, and out slid a frozen treat.
He called it the Epsicle. Epperson plus icicle.
Years later he sold them at a California beach park and patented it in nineteen twenty-four.
But his own kids kept calling it Pop's sicle.
And that's how a forgotten cup became the popsicle.
What flavor would you have left on that porch? Tell me in the comments.
So next time you unwrap one, think about it.

title: 3 Tricks to Open a Stuck Jar Lid
hook: Before you give up on that stuck jar, try these 3 tricks you already have the stuff for.
script:
Before you give up on that stuck jar, try these three tricks you already have the stuff for.
Each beats a different reason lids stick.
Trick one: grip. Wrap the lid in a dish towel or wear a rubber glove.
No slipping, so all your twist goes into the lid.
Trick two: heat. Run just the lid under hot tap water for about a minute.
Metal expands as it warms, so the lid loosens its hold.
Dry it, then twist with the towel.
Trick three: tap around the lid's edge with the back of a spoon.
That can loosen sticky food gluing the lid.
Bonus for a new jar: gently pry the lid edge with a bottle opener until it pops.
That pop is the vacuum seal letting go.
So that's grip, heat and a tap, and none of them need big muscles.
Which trick are you trying first? Tell me in the comments.
And next time a jar fights back, remember...

Tiny channels between its scales carry water to its mouth.
Number one: the kangaroo rat. It rarely, if ever, drinks water.

title: Jack-o'-Lantern History in 60 Seconds
hook: Before you carve your pumpkin, you should know why the first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips.
script:
Before you carve your pumpkin, you should know why the first jack-o'-lanterns were turnips.
Here's how Halloween's famous decoration swapped vegetables.
Long ago in Ireland, people carved faces into big turnips and potatoes.
Scotland used turnips too, and in England, large beets.
They put a light inside and set them by windows and doors, to scare away wandering spirits.
Picture a small, wrinkly turnip face glowing at you. Way creepier than a pumpkin.
The name comes from an Irish folktale about a trickster called Stingy Jack.
His ghostly light was Jack of the Lantern, later shortened to jack-o'-lantern.
Then families from Ireland, Scotland and England moved to America.
There they found pumpkins, which are native to the Americas.
Bigger, hollow, and way easier to carve than a rock-hard turnip.
So your jack-o'-lantern is a pumpkin because it was an upgrade.
Would you dare carve a turnip this year?
Either way, here's the one thing to remember this October.

script:

Three questions, three seconds each. Keep score.
Three, two, one.
Australia! It's almost four thousand kilometers from side to side.

Most flat maps stretch places near the poles, so Greenland looks way bigger than it is.
So your map wasn't lying on purpose. You just can't flatten a round planet perfectly.

title: 3 Tricks to Find North When You're Lost
hook: Before you get lost without signal, you need these 3 ways to find north.
script:
Before you get lost without signal, you need these three ways to find north.
All you need is the sky and a stick.
Way one: the sun rises roughly east and sets roughly west.
Rarely exactly, so it's just a quick first guess.
Way two: push a stick into flat ground and mark the tip of its shadow.
Wait ten to fifteen minutes, and mark the tip again.
The first mark is west, the second is east, anywhere on Earth.
Left foot on the first mark, right on the second: you're facing north.
Way three, at night in the northern half of the world: find the Big Dipper.
Follow the two stars at the end of its bowl about five times their gap.
That's the North Star. Walk toward it, and you're heading north.
Three ways to find north, and none of them need a battery.
Which one would you trust if you were lost?
And next time your phone hits one percent, remember.

You'd never guess that before alarm clocks, someone got paid to shoot peas at your window.

Before fridges, crews sawed giant blocks of ice from frozen lakes to keep for summer.
Number four, pinsetter.
Bowling alleys paid kids to sit at the end of the lane and reset every pin by hand.
Dodging bowling balls came free.
Number three, lector.
In cigar factories, workers paid someone to read newspapers and novels out loud while they rolled.
A human audiobook.
Number two, swan upper.
Every summer on England's River Thames, crews row along counting swans and shout "All up!"
And yes, that still happens.
Number one, knocker-upper.
In industrial Britain, they tapped on windows with long poles to wake people for work.
One London woman, Mary Smith, shot dried peas through a tube instead.
Which of these five jobs would you actually sign up for?

title: Quick Weather Quiz: 2 Fakes, 1 Real
hook: Why do you believe lightning never strikes the same place twice? Real or fake?
script:
Why do you believe lightning never strikes the same place twice? Real or fake?
Three weather facts, three seconds each. Call it before I do.
Fact one, lightning never strikes the same place twice.
Three, two, one.
Fake! Tall, pointy things get hit again and again.
The Empire State Building gets struck about twenty-three times a year.
Fact two, lightning is hotter than the surface of the sun.
Three, two, one.
Real! A bolt can heat the air to about fifty thousand degrees Fahrenheit.
That's around five times hotter than the sun's surface.
Fact three, it can be too cold to snow.
Three, two, one.
Fake! It can snow when it's bitterly cold, but cold air holds less water, so you get less snow.
So there's your answer key: two fakes and one real.
How many did you get right, zero, one, two or three?
And if you missed fact one, ask yourself again.

title: The Eiffel Tower Had a 20-Year Expiry Date
hook: Before you visit Paris, you should know the Eiffel Tower had an expiry date.
script:
Before you visit Paris, you should know the Eiffel Tower had an expiry date.
Here's how it almost came down, and what saved it.
The tower opened for the World's Fair in eighteen eighty-nine.
But Gustave Eiffel's deal only let him use the land for twenty years.
After that, Paris could take it down.
So Eiffel needed a reason to keep it.
His answer? Science.
He backed weather and air resistance experiments up there.
Then in eighteen ninety-eight, a Morse code radio message was sent from the tower across Paris.
Suddenly, the city's tallest structure looked like the perfect giant antenna.
Army radio tests from the top reached farther and farther.
By nineteen-oh-nine, a permanent radio station sat right beneath it.
So in nineteen-ten, Eiffel's deal was extended by seventy years.
That's how the tower beat its expiry date: it became an antenna.
Did you know the Eiffel Tower almost came down, yes or no?
If you said no, here's your reminder.

title: How Do They Get Graphite Inside Pencils?
hook: Before you sharpen another pencil, you should know there's no lead inside it.
script:
Before you sharpen another pencil, you should know there's no lead inside it.
Here's what's in there, and how it gets in without a drill.
Centuries ago, English miners found a shiny black mineral and thought it was lead.
It was actually graphite, but the name stuck.
Today, graphite is ground into powder and mixed with clay.
More clay makes it harder and lighter, more graphite makes it softer and darker.
The paste is squeezed into thin strings and baked hard.
Now the wood.
A machine cuts grooves into a flat wooden slat.
Glue goes in, then the cores are laid in, one by one.
A second grooved slat goes on top, like a sandwich.
It's clamped, dried overnight, then cut into separate pencils and painted.
So that's how the lead gets in: it's glued into a wooden sandwich, and it's never been lead.
What color was the pencil you used most in school?
Whatever color it was, it had graphite inside, so next time.

title: Why Your Paper Plane Nosedives (3 Fixes)
hook: Why does your paper plane always nosedive, and how do you stop it?
script:
Why does your paper plane always nosedive, and how do you stop it?
Here are three tricks to make it glide farther, and each takes seconds.
Trick one, make every crease razor sharp.
Run your fingernail along each fold.
Tight folds keep the shape clean.
Trick two, check that both wings match.
Hold the nose toward you and look straight down the middle.
If one wing is higher, the plane will roll or spin, so fix it first.
Trick three, the nosedive fix.
Pinch the back edge of each wing and curl it up, just a tiny bit.
Those little flaps act like elevators and help lift the nose.
If it now swoops up and stalls, flatten them a touch.
Throw it gently and level.
That's how you stop the nosedive: sharp creases, matching wings, and a tiny curl at the back.
What's the farthest your paper plane has ever flown?
If the answer is two feet, you already know the question.

The trap caught nothing, because the fake town had turned real.

script:
Why do your fresh eggs peel the worst, and what can you do before you boil them?
Here are three tricks for eggs that slip right out of the shell.
Trick one, use older eggs.
Super fresh eggs cling to their shells, so week-old eggs peel easier.
Trick two, start them in boiling water, not cold.
Gently lower cold eggs from the fridge into water that's already bubbling.
In kitchen tests, that starting temperature made the biggest difference.
A slow start gives the egg white more time to stick to the shell.
Trick three, the ice bath.
Once they're cooked, move them into ice water and let them chill for fifteen minutes.
It also stops that dent at the bottom.
So that's why fresh eggs peel the worst, and the fix is older eggs, a hot start and an icy finish.

title: Why Are Bubbles Always Round? 1 Simple Rule
hook: You can make a square wand, but you'll never blow a square bubble, and here's why.
script:
You can make a square wand, but you'll never blow a square bubble, and here's why.
Here's the simple rule that makes every bubble round.
A bubble is a thin soapy skin wrapped around air.
That skin is always pulling itself tighter, like a stretched balloon.
Scientists call that pull surface tension.
It wants the smallest skin possible to hold the air inside.
And here's the math part.
Of every shape, a sphere wraps the most space with the least surface.
A cube holding the same air would need more skin.
So whatever your wand's shape, a floating bubble pulls into a ball.
When two bubbles touch, they share a flat wall between them.
And a giant bubble a few meters wide can sag under its own weight.
So that's why you'll never blow a square bubble, the soap always picks a sphere.
What's the biggest bubble you've ever blown?
Tell me, and if you've got a square wand, go try it.

title: 5 Real English Words That Sound Made Up

script:
You've been saying confused, but there's a funnier real word, and you'll never stop using it.

Number five, lollygag.
It means to goof off and waste time, and it's been around since at least eighteen sixty-two.
Number four, kerfuffle.
It's a big fuss over something small, and it comes from an old Scottish word, curfuffle.
Number three, cattywampus.
It means crooked, or sitting at a weird angle, and funny enough, it mostly has nothing to do with cats.
Number two, bumfuzzle.
It's a real word for confused, and you'll mostly hear it in the southern United States.
Number one, flibbertigibbet.
It means a silly, flighty, chatty person, and Shakespeare used it in King Lear.
So that's your funnier word, next time you're confused, just say you're bumfuzzled.

Try bumfuzzle first, because once you've said it, you'll never go back to saying confused.

title: Why Golf Balls Have 300+ Dimples
hook: Why does a golf ball have dimples? You'd never guess the reason until you see the air.
script:
Why does a golf ball have dimples? You'd never guess the reason until you see the air.
Here's how tiny dents make it fly farther.
A typical golf ball has three hundred to five hundred dimples.
Now picture a perfectly smooth ball flying through the air.
The air peels off its back early and leaves a big, messy wake.
That wake works like a brake.
Dimples stir up a thin layer of air that hugs the ball longer.
So the wake shrinks, and there's less drag.
Add backspin, and the dimples help with lift too.
Fun part, early golfers noticed their beat-up, nicked balls flew farther than smooth new ones.
So that's the reason, the dents help the air hold on, and a dimpled ball can fly about twice as far as a smooth one.
How many dimples do you think are on a golf ball?
Go count one, and next time someone asks why a golf ball has dimples, you'll know.

title: Play-Doh Was Wallpaper Cleaner for 20 Years
hook: You've squished it, but you've never known Play-Doh started out cleaning soot off walls in Cincinnati.
script:
You've squished it, but you've never known Play-Doh started out cleaning soot off walls in Cincinnati.
Here's how a wall cleaner became a famous toy.
In the nineteen-thirties, many homes burned coal, which left sooty grime on wallpaper.
So a Cincinnati soap company called Kutol sold a doughy putty you'd roll over walls to lift the dirt.
It was a wall cleaner for about twenty years.
But after World War Two, families switched to oil and gas heat.
Less soot, fewer dirty walls, and sales slid.
Then a nursery school teacher named Kay Zufall had her class make crafts with it.
She told her brother-in-law, Joe McVicker, who ran the company, to sell it as a toy.
In the mid nineteen-fifties, it got a new name, Play-Doh.
So that's the twist, the toy in your hands was made to clean walls.
What's the best thing you've made out of Play-Doh?
So next time you squish it, think of a sooty wall in Cincinnati.

script:

Rub bar soap or petroleum jelly on the hinge, then swing the door.

Trick two, the real fix.
Tap a nail up under the hinge pin and pull the pin out.
Scrub it with steel wool, oil it, and tap it back in.
Trick three, find the troublemaker.
Still squeaking? Pull one pin at a time and test the door.
When the squeak stops, that's the hinge to fix.
So that's how you stop it for good, clean the pin, oil it, check every hinge.
Which door in your house squeaks the loudest?
Because if you only sprayed it, you might hear it again soon.

title: The Sleep Jump Up to 70% of People Get
hook: Why does your body jump right before you fall asleep, and what is your brain actually doing?
script:
Why does your body jump right before you fall asleep, and what is your brain actually doing?
Here's what happens in that split second.
That sudden jolt has a name, it's called a hypnic jerk.
Sleep experts say up to seventy percent of people get them.
As you drift off, your muscles relax, all at once.
One idea is that your brain misreads all that relaxing as falling.
So it fires your muscles to catch you.
That's why it often comes with a quick falling feeling.
Another idea goes back to our tree-sleeping ancestors, where a slip meant a real fall.
Scientists say that one's still a guess, though.
Stress, caffeine and too little sleep can make them happen more.
And for most people, they're harmless.
So that's what your brain is doing, it thinks you're falling, and it tries to catch you.
Which do you get more, the jump or the falling feeling?
Because tonight, right before you drift off, it might happen again.

title: Top 5 Animals That Play Dead Like Pros

script:

Here are the five best fakers in nature.
Number five, the death-feigning beetle.
It tucks in its legs and looks just like a pebble.
Number four, a tiny frog from Brazil.
It flips over, shuts its eyes, then peeks to see if you're gone.
Number three, Livingstone's cichlid, an African lake fish.
It lies on its side looking dead, and when small fish come close, it strikes.
Number two, the eastern hognose snake.
It rolls over, tongue out, and if you flip it upright, it rolls right back.
Number one, the Virginia opossum.
It goes stiff, tongue out, and even gives off a stinky smell, sometimes for hours.
And it's not even trying, it happens automatically.
So the snake never quits when flipped, but the possum wins, it even smells the part.
Which of these would fool you best?
Next time an animal lies perfectly still, ask yourself.

title: How a Dog Walk Invented Velcro in 1941
hook: Before you rip open your Velcro again, know that it started with burrs stuck to a Swiss inventor's dog.
script:
Before you rip open your Velcro again, know that it started with burrs stuck to a Swiss inventor's dog.
Here's how one walk became the strap on your shoes.
In nineteen forty-one, engineer George de Mestral went hunting in the Jura mountains with his dog.
Back home, his pants and his dog were covered in burrs.
George put a burr under a microscope.
He saw hundreds of tiny hooks, grabbing little loops in fabric and fur.
Could he make a fastener that works the same way?
With a weaver in France, it took nearly eight years to copy.
One side got hooks, the other got loops.
He named it Velcro, from the French words for velvet and hook.
It was patented in the United States in nineteen fifty-five.
Later, NASA even used it on the Apollo missions.
So that's how a dog covered in burrs gave you Velcro.

title: Why Your Skipping Stone Sinks (3 Fixes)
hook: Why does your skipping stone die after one bounce? Scientists in France actually found out.
script:
Why does your skipping stone die after one bounce? Scientists in France actually found out.
Here are three fixes backed by physics.
Fix one, pick the right stone.
Look for one that's flat, smooth and fits in your palm.
A flat stone skims the surface instead of plunging in.
Fix two, tilt it.
Researchers found the best angle between stone and water is about twenty degrees.
That's a slight nose-up tilt, not flat and not steep.
Fix three, spin it.
Snap your wrist so the stone spins fast as it leaves your hand.
Spin works like a gyroscope, keeping the stone steady so it doesn't wobble and dive.
And throw it low and fast, so it hits the water hard enough to bounce back up.
So that's why your stone sank, wrong stone, wrong angle, or no spin.
What's the most skips you've ever gotten?

title: Can You Do These 3 Body Tricks?

script:

Stuck? Little tendon bridges tie it to its neighbors, so it can't lift alone.
Trick two. Circle your right foot clockwise.

Did your foot flip? For lots of people, it does.
Scientists aren't sure why, but one idea is your brain links plans for limbs on the same side.
Trick three. Roll your tongue into a U.
Roughly sixty-five to eighty-one percent of people can.
Textbooks called it a simple gene, but identical twins don't always match.
So now you know why your finger sticks, your foot flips, and your tongue might not roll.

script:

title: Why Leaves Change Color in 60 Seconds
hook: Why do leaves change color? You'd never guess, but the yellow was there before fall even started.
script:
Why do leaves change color? You'd never guess, but the yellow was there before fall even started.
Here's what's happening inside a leaf.
All summer, leaves are packed with chlorophyll.
That's the green stuff that helps the tree turn sunlight into food.
So much of it that it hides the other colors.
But as days get shorter and cooler, trees make less chlorophyll, and the old green breaks down.
Then the hidden yellows and oranges show up.
They're pigments called carotenoids, and they were there all along, hiding behind the green.
Reds and purples work differently.
Trees like red and sugar maples make them fresh in late summer and fall.
They're called anthocyanins, and the first frost can help bring them out.
So yellow leaves aren't changing color, they're finally showing it.
What's the most colorful tree on your street? Tell me in the comments.

title: Why the Hollywood Sign Lost 4 Letters
hook: Why is the Hollywood sign missing four letters? You'd never guess, but it was built to sell houses.
script:
Why is the Hollywood sign missing four letters? You'd never guess, but it was built to sell houses.
Here's the true story.
In nineteen twenty-three, developers were selling homes in the hills above Los Angeles.
Their neighborhood was called Hollywoodland.
So they built a huge sign spelling it, with letters fifty feet tall.
It had about four thousand light bulbs and cost twenty-one thousand dollars.
The plan? Take it down after about a year and a half.
But nobody did.
Over the years, it got old and shabby.
In nineteen forty-nine, the local chamber of commerce fixed it up.
And they removed the last four letters, L, A, N, D.
Now it stood for the whole area, not just one neighborhood.
In nineteen seventy-eight, worn-out letters were replaced with sturdier new ones.
So the world's most famous sign started as a temporary ad.

title: How Popcorn Pops: 135 PSI Inside One Kernel
hook: Before a popcorn kernel pops, the pressure inside builds to about nine times the air around you. Here's why.
script:
Before a popcorn kernel pops, the pressure inside builds to about nine times the air around you. Here's why.
Let's look inside one tiny kernel.
Each kernel holds a drop of water and soft starch, inside a tough shell called the hull.
Heat it, and that water turns into steam.
But the hull won't let the steam out.
So the kernel keeps heating, to around three hundred forty-seven degrees Fahrenheit.
Inside, the starch turns into a hot, gooey gel.
The pressure climbs to about one hundred thirty-five pounds per square inch.
Then, pop! The hull bursts.
The starch puffs up and sets into that fluffy shape, up to fifty times bigger.
And the jump? The first starch out acts like a tiny leg kicking it up.
So that's why popcorn pops: trapped steam builds pressure until the hull gives way.
What's your favorite popcorn topping? Tell me in the comments.
And next time you hear that first pop, think about what happens before it.

title: How a 1943 Accident Became the Slinky
hook: You've played with a Slinky, but you've never heard how a naval engineer found it by accident.
script:

In nineteen forty-three, engineer Richard James was testing springs to steady instruments on ships.
One day, he dropped one.
Instead of just landing, it kept moving, flipping end over end.
He thought, wait, that could be a toy.
His wife Betty flipped through a dictionary and found the name Slinky.
They made four hundred, and a Philadelphia store called Gimbels agreed to sell them in nineteen forty-five.
At first, nobody bought one.
So Richard showed the spring walking down a ramp.
All four hundred sold out in about ninety minutes, at a dollar each.
So the Slinky really was an accident, a dropped spring that wouldn't stop.

title: How to Soften Stale Bread: 3 Easy Tricks
hook: Never put your bread in the fridge. Here's why, and three ways to rescue a stale loaf before you toss it.
script:
Never put your bread in the fridge. Here's why, and three ways to rescue a stale loaf before you toss it.
Let's make your bread soft again.
Bread goes stale when its starch dries out and hardens, and cold fridge air speeds that up.
Trick one, the oven.
Dampen the crust, wrap the loaf in foil, and warm it at three hundred degrees Fahrenheit for ten to fifteen minutes.
Then unwrap it for five more minutes to crisp the crust.
Trick two, the microwave.
Wrap a slice in a damp towel and heat it in ten-second bursts. Eat it warm.
Trick three, steam.
Set the bread in a colander over boiling water for about five minutes.
To keep it fresh, use a sealed bag, or freeze it.
So that's how you rescue stale bread: oven, microwave or steam, and never the fridge.

In America, it's a fluffy bread roll. Good luck dunking that.
And number one, pants. In America, pants go on your legs.
In Britain, pants are underwear. The leg ones are trousers.
So nice pants in London sounds like you can see their underwear.

title: 1 Stone Coin Sank. It Still Counted

script:

The true story of money too big to move.
Yap is a group of Pacific islands in Micronesia.
For a long time, people there used giant stone wheels called rai as money.
They were carved on Palau, about four hundred kilometers away, and brought back by canoe.
The biggest one left is about twelve feet wide and weighs around four thousand kilos.
Not exactly pocket-sized.
So the stones stay put, and everyone remembers who owns each one.
When one changes hands, only its list of owners changes.
Then one big stone was dropped into the sea on the way home.
But everyone agreed it was still down there, so people kept trading it.
So a coin on the seafloor still counted.
Would you trust money you could never see? Tell me in the comments.
Because somewhere down there, that stone is still worth something.

title: The Space Signal Heard Once in 1977

script:
You could listen to the sky for almost fifty years and never hear it again, but in nineteen seventy-seven, Ohio's Big Ear did.
This is the true story of the Wow signal.
August fifteenth, nineteen seventy-seven. Big Ear, a radio telescope, is scanning space.
It didn't move. Earth's spin swept the sky past it.
It caught a strong, sharp signal from the direction of Sagittarius.
It lasted seventy-two seconds, exactly as long as one spot of sky stays in view.
The printout showed a strange code: six, E, Q, U, J, five.
Letters meant extra strong.
An astronomer circled it in red ink and wrote: Wow.
Telescopes went back again and again.
Nothing.
In twenty twenty-four, scientists suggested a magnetar flare may have made a hydrogen cloud flash.
It's still just an idea.
So that's the Wow signal: seventy-two seconds, one word, no repeat.
Nature, or something else? Tell me in the comments.
Because we're still listening, and so far, nothing.

title: Why Pineapple Tingles Your Tongue: 1 Enzyme
hook: Before you bite that fresh pineapple, know this: it's breaking down proteins on your tongue.
script:
Before you bite that fresh pineapple, know this: it's breaking down proteins on your tongue.
Here's what's going on.
Fresh pineapple is packed with an enzyme called bromelain.
Enzymes are tiny helpers that speed up chemical reactions.
Bromelain's favorite job is chopping up proteins.
And the surface of your mouth? It's full of proteins.
So while you chew, it nibbles at that surface, and you feel a tingle.
Pineapple's acid makes the sting feel stronger.
The good news? Your mouth repairs itself, so it fades.
Now here's the cool part. Heat wrecks bromelain.
That's why grilled or canned pineapple doesn't sting the same way.
It's also why fresh pineapple can stop gelatin from setting.
Gelatin is a protein too, so bromelain chops it up.
So yes, fresh pineapple really is breaking down proteins on your tongue, just a little.

And next time you grab a fresh slice, remember this.

title: Why Wombat Poop Is a Cube: 1 Weird Gut
hook: Before you laugh, wombat poop is actually a real science mystery. Why is it a cube?
script:
Before you laugh, wombat poop is actually a real science mystery. Why is it a cube?
Here's how a round animal makes square poop.
Wombats are the only animals known to poop cubes.
So a team at Georgia Tech looked inside a wombat's gut.
Here's the trick: near the very end, the gut wall isn't the same all the way around.
Some parts are stiff, and some parts are stretchy.
As the poop squeezes through, the stiff parts flatten the sides and the stretchy parts make the corners.
And wombat poop is really dry, so the cubes hold their shape.
Wombats leave them on rocks and logs like little notes. One idea is cubes don't roll off.
The research even won an Ig Nobel Prize in twenty nineteen.

Three tricks that work, and one popular one that's a myth.

Ice only touches the can in spots. Water hugs the whole can and pulls heat away faster.

Gently roll the can in the bath, so the warm drink in the middle moves to the cold edges.

title: The Bank Built From the Mail in 1916

title: Why the Ocean Is Salty in 60 Seconds
hook: If you spread the ocean's salt over the land, it'd pile up as high as a forty-story building.
script:
If you spread the ocean's salt over the land, it'd pile up as high as a forty-story building.
So where does all that salt come from? Let's follow it.
It starts with rain. Raindrops pick up a little carbon dioxide, which makes them slightly acidic.
That gentle acid slowly wears down rocks, freeing tiny bits of minerals.
Rivers carry those minerals to the sea, in amounts too small for you to taste.
In the ocean, the sun evaporates water, but the minerals can't leave with it. So they build up.
Hot vents on the seafloor add even more minerals from below.
Over a very long time, seawater became about three and a half percent salt, mostly the same stuff as table salt.
So the ocean's salty because it's the end of the line: rivers bring the salt, and only the water leaves.
Which do you like swimming in more, the salty ocean or a freshwater lake?

title: How A Click Pen Works in 2 Clicks
hook: You've clicked a pen thousands of times, but you've never seen what spins inside it.
script:
You've clicked a pen thousands of times, but you've never seen what spins inside it.
Your thumb pushes a plunger with tiny teeth.
They press a little crown with slanted teeth, called a cam.
The slants twist it one step.
Let go, and the spring lifts it onto a ledge. Tip locked out.
Click again, and it slips off the ledge and twists once more.
Now it misses the ledge, and the spring pulls the tip in.
Two twists, one spring, every single click.

title: Guess the Real Names of 3 Tiny Things

script:

Three tiny things, three seconds each, then the real name.
Number one: the plastic tip on the end of your shoelace. Three, two, one.
It's an aglet. It stops the lace from fraying.
The word comes from an old French word meaning needle.
Number two: the little dot on top of a lowercase i or j. Three, two, one.
It's called a tittle. Yes, really.
It shows up in the old phrase "every jot and tittle," meaning every tiny detail.
Number three: the little groove between your nose and your top lip. Three, two, one.
That's your philtrum. Most mammals have one, and its name comes from an ancient Greek word for love charm.
So there they are: aglet, tittle, philtrum, three names for things you see every single day.

So the water climbs, pocket after pocket.
Too steep, and it spills back down.
At the top, every turn pours out a splash.

title: How 15 GPS Rocks Solved a Desert Mystery
hook: You'd think rocks can't move by themselves. In Death Valley, they left tracks hundreds of feet long.
script:
You'd think rocks can't move by themselves. In Death Valley, they left tracks hundreds of feet long.
Here's the true story of how scientists finally caught them moving.
On a dry, flat lakebed called Racetrack Playa, rocks sit at the end of long, wandering trails.
Nobody had ever seen one move.
Since the nineteen-forties, scientists wondered what pushed them. Wind? Mud? Something stranger?
So a team of researchers fitted fifteen rocks with GPS trackers and set up cameras.
They thought they might be waiting for years.
In December twenty-thirteen, rain made a shallow pond there, and it froze overnight.
In the sun, the ice cracked into huge panels thinner than a phone.
A light breeze pushed the panels, and they shoved the rocks along a few inches per second.
So the rocks never moved themselves. Thin ice and a light wind did the pushing.
Would you have guessed ice, in one of the hottest places on Earth?
Because for a long time, everyone just figured

title: Which Food Lasts Longest? 3-Second Quiz
hook: Think you know which food lasts longest? You get three seconds before each answer.
script:
Think you know which food lasts longest? You get three seconds before each answer.
Three food questions, and at least one answer sounds wrong.
Question one. Honey or a Twinkie: which lasts longer on the shelf?
Three, two, one.
It's honey. Archaeologists have found pots of honey in ancient Egyptian tombs, and sealed honey basically never spoils.
Question two. True or false: a Twinkie lasts forever.
Three, two, one.
False. Its official shelf life is about forty-five days. That's long for a little cake, but nowhere near forever.
Question three. True or false: swallowed gum stays in your stomach for seven years.
Three, two, one.
False. Your body can't break down the gum base, but it still passes through in a few days, like other things you can't digest.
So the food that lasts the longest is honey, by thousands of years.
How many did you get right: zero, one, two, or all three?
Now try it on a friend, and ask them

title: How to Remove a Stripped Screw: 3 Tricks
hook: You're probably making that stripped screw worse. Here's how to get it out before you ruin the wood.
script:
You're probably making that stripped screw worse. Here's how to get it out before you ruin the wood.
Three tricks, from easiest to the one that almost never fails.
First, stop spinning harder. Every slip grinds the head smoother.
Trick one, the rubber band. Lay a wide rubber band over the screw head, press your screwdriver into it, and turn slowly.
The rubber fills the worn slots and gives the tip grip.
Trick two, pliers. If the head sticks up, clamp locking pliers on and twist it out slowly.
Trick three, a screw extractor. It's a cheap drill bit with backward threads.
Put on safety glasses, drill a small hole in the screw head, then run the extractor in reverse until it bites and backs the screw out.
So that's it: rubber band first, pliers second, extractor last, and the screw comes out without wrecking the wood.
What's the most stubborn screw you've ever had to fight?
